paper_title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multi-agent architectures are applied to language models for reasoning and code generation [1, 2]. Frameworks allow multiple model instances to debate or decompose problems through communication [35]. Evaluating multi-agent systems without compute parity obscures whether gains stem from coordination or inference budget. When topology of agents communicates across rounds, it consumes roughly times the test tokens and inference cost of greedy baseline, which confounds communication with compute scaling. Because repeated sampling, majority voting, and longer reasoning traces improve accuracy without communication between models [68], isolating the effect of coordination requires holding inference compute constant. Studies that control or audit inference budgets reach different conclusions depending on which resource is held constant and what task structure is evaluated. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Prior multi-agent frameworks report gains over single models on reasoning, coding, and benchmark deduction [35, 14], with scaling in agent count popularized by Li et al. [15], who observed that independent sampling and majority voting alone (Agent Forest) scale performance with the number of agents; our synthesis tests whether inter-agent communication provides gains beyond this sample multiplicity. In most of these evaluations, however, the single-agent baseline is single greedy pass, which confounds architectural communication with the accuracy gains known to come from repeated sampling and extended test-time reasoning [68]. Isolating the effect of coordination requires holding inference compute constant and measuring the sampling gap against compute-matched baselines. 3 Controlled audits challenge unconditional multi-agent superiority. When budgets are matched on thinking tokens, single agent matches or outperforms debate across reasoning benchmarks [9]. Evaluating 260 configurations that use tools across six benchmarks in Nature Machine Intelligence, Kim et al. [10] report that multi-agent gains diminish as baseline model competence rises, turning negative beyond 45% threshold. Ferreira et al. [16] evaluate 23 models across eleven vendor families with 5,500 runs with generation-budget matching, finding that debate often ties or trails majority voting once generation budgets are matched. Bertalaniˇc and Fortuna [17] observe that multi-agent consensus consumes 2.13.4 more tokens than self-correction without improving accuracy, while nominal agent scaling exhibits coordination degradation analogous to the Ringelmann effect [18]. In shared-context token budgeting, Nguyen et al. [19] observe that self-consistency matches or outperforms deployed debate in 93% of window-matched settings, and Ann et al. [20] identify an interaction tax under matched budgets on verifier-scored tasks. Matching definitions diverge across papers: some audits equate internal scratchpad tokens while ignoring prompt inflation; others match iteration counts or monitor monetary API spend [11, 12]. At comparable compute read off Pareto fronts on MMLU-Pro, Wunderlich et al. [12] observe that debate and mixture-of-agents outperform self-consistency by +1.3 and +2.7 percentage points, reporting positive accuracy differences on dense multiple choice items under matched compute. system matched on token count can remain unmatched on execution latency or financial cost. Recent benchmarking efforts such as the Holistic Agent Leaderboard [21] emphasize standardized multidimensional evaluation. The resource vector with six dimensions formalizes these reporting distinctions (Section 4). Kapoor et al. [22] argue that agent evaluations must be cost-controlled and report, on codegeneration benchmark, that simple baselines can match complex agent architectures at lower cost. Wang et al. [23] likewise compare multi-agent debate with self-consistency under token budgets. The resource vector with six dimensions formalizes these cost-aware principles into standardized accounting framework that we apply across primary studies. Closest prior empirical work compares debate-style systems with single-agent and selfconsistency baselines on sets of benchmarks. Smit et al. [24], Zhang et al. [25], and Yang et al. [26] differ in what they hold fixed. Yang et al. give self-consistency, refinement, and debate the same maximum of 16 samples. Smit et al. report the best and the median score over hyperparameter configurations, whereas the tables of Zhang et al. do not report matched tokens or cost. In our extraction of their tables, debate-based systems are ahead of the sampled baseline in minority of contrasts (19% for Zhang et al., 17% for Yang et al., 21% for Smit et al.; Section 5). To our knowledge none of these papers places its results beside studies with other matching conditions (thinking tokens, iterations, cost, agent count) in one resource-accounting framework, or compares the same multi-agent systems against greedy and sampled baselines across studies. That placement is what we add. Statistical comparisons of classifiers [27] and error bar practices for LLM evaluations [28] address variance within benchmark, but not synthesis across papers. Dependent effect sizes within study are handled by multilevel models [29, 30] with robust variance estimation [31, 32]. Raw accuracy differences are bounded and ceiling compressed [33], which motivates our log odds scale. Task decomposability governs multi-agent returns. On MASBENCH, orchestrator architectures achieve gains on parallel tasks, but fail on ordered sequential deduction where single chain of thought scores higher [34]. Routing topology also affects token efficiency under partial observability [35]. Zhu et al. [36] report that while unguided homogeneous debate often underperforms simple majority voting, confidence-weighted aggregation and diverse initializations outperform both vanilla debate and majority voting across six reasoning QA benchmarks. Framing debate as collaborative nonzero-sum game with supportive critique oriented toward downstream judge improves error 4 detection and oversight accuracy at matched token budgets [37]. While recent surveys review agent benchmarks [38], prior work does not synthesize effect sizes across distinct matching conditions and baseline sampling strategies. We analyze paired contrasts extracted from primary empirical tables across the literature. Single-agent baselines and aggregation. Wang et al. [39] find that single agent with strong prompts almost matches the best discussion approach on wide range of reasoning tasks, and that multi-agent discussion is better only when the prompt contains no demonstration. This is an early baseline-strength result for discussion. Yang et al. [40] note that most multi-agent frameworks aggregate by majority vote, which is brittle when agents share correlated biases, and propose an evidence-structured adjudicator. Correlated answers are the case that Proposition 3.2(2) describes through the effective number of independent answers. Reproducibility standards and noise floors. Pattnayak and Bhatia [41] audit 55 LLM pipeline papers published from 2022 to 2025 for evaluation artifacts and report that randomness controls are missing in 75% and intermediate execution traces in 61% of them. Their coding concerns artifact availability, whereas the audit here concerns baseline strength. Masters et al. [42] propose rollout cards, which preserve the rollout record behind reported score together with the reporting rules and drops manifests used to compute it, and document reporting-rule differences in cost and token accounting. The PACE resource vector can be written as compute block in cards annotation namespace and reporting-rule registry (pace report --export-rollout-card, with an example in Section D). Kaliyev and Maryanskyy [43] propose paired noise-floor protocol for coordination gains. On one model and one benchmark they find paired gaps between configuration-equivalent protocols that range from 3 to +18 percentage points across two seeds of 100 trials. noise floor of this kind and baseline-strength audit address different threats: the first asks how large difference must be to exceed run-to-run variation, and the second asks whether the baseline received comparable compute.

sections.title: 3.1 Context Crowding and the Data Processing Bound
sections.content: Tran and Kiela [9] invoke an information-theoretic bound rooted in the Data Processing Inequality: given fixed budget of thinking tokens and uncorrupted context retention, passing intermediate reasoning traces through an inter-agent communication channel cannot increase mutual information with the target solution relative to allocating all tokens directly to internal single-agent thinking. In empirical evaluation, this bound operates under two specific conditions: (i) the total reasoningtoken budget is held constant, and (ii) the single agents reasoning capacity does not degrade over longer contexts. When single-agent reasoning suffers context fragmentation, or when tasks require partitioned contexts, parallel external tools, or sandboxed execution, multi-agent topologies can circumvent this constraint. Rather than relying on asymptotic information bounds, we model the operational trade-off directly through scaffolding overhead and context crowding.

sections.title: 3.5 Four-Category Baseline Taxonomy
sections.content: To prevent conflating sample multiplicity with compute control, we organize empirical comparisons into four baseline categories: 1. Category (Greedy Single-Pass Baselines): Multi-agent architectures are compared against single forward pass (N = 1, = 1). This comparison provides baseline performance but confounds coordination with sample count and test-time token expenditure. 2. Category (Sample-Matched Baselines): The number of generation trajectories is matched (k = ), such as in k-sample self-consistency with majority voting. Total tokens, latency, and monetary costs remain unconstrained. This category evaluates whether communication provides advantages beyond independent sample multiplicity. 3. Category (Resource-Matched Baselines): declared resource constraint is held equal be- ), matched sample or tween conditions, such as matched thinking tokens (RMAS reason = RSAS iteration ceilings (RMAS ), or matched monetary budgets (RMAS cost = RSAS cost ). = RSAS reason sample sample 4. Category (Pareto Frontier Sweeps): Accuracy is evaluated against inference expenditure across parametric sweep of configurations, tracing empirical accuracycost or accuracy latency frontiers (e.g., Wunderlich et al. [12]). Comparing multi-agent teams against greedy single-agent baselines mixes two phenomena: variance reduction from drawing multiple stochastic trajectories, and coordination through communication. Under token matching or iteration controls (Category C), the comparison holds compute 10 constant, isolating coordination efficiency. Under matching on agent count (Category B), the comparison reflects unconstrained sample multiplicity, where majority voting over independent samples matches or exceeds debate without communication overhead [13, 15].

sections.title: 4 The Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE) Protocol and
sections.content: the Resource Vector comparison between multi-agent system (MAS) and single-agent system (SAS) requires disclosing the compute resources being equated. Rather than reducing compute to single scalar, we formalize the resource vector with six dimensions: = Rreason, Rtoken, Rcost, Rlat, Rsample, Rsys, where each component measures distinct test-time compute constraint: (11) 1. Rreason (Thinking Tokens): Tokens generated inside reasoning or scratchpad blocks across all calls. 2. Rtoken (Total Tokens): Cumulative input, output, prompt, and scaffold tokens across all calls and rounds. 3. Rcost (Monetary Cost): Total financial expenditure based on published API pricing or normalized FLOPs. 4. Rlat (Execution Latency): Serialized execution time, accounting for network synchronization and delays across interaction rounds. 5. Rsample (Sample / Instance Count): Total number of model forward passes drawn and aggregated. 6. Rsys (System Scaffolding & Tools): Invocations of external compilers, retrieval engines, bash tools, and system prompt overhead. For any empirical comparison, each dimension of is assigned one of four verification states: Strictly Controlled: Identical budget enforced between MAS and SAS (e.g., Tran & Kiela thinking tokens). Approximately Matched: Controlled within bounded thresholds (e.g., Kim et al. maximum iterations; Wunderlich et al. compute budget sweeps). Unmatched (Measured): Audited and reported, but allowed to diverge (e.g., Jwalapuram et al. dollar costs). Unreported (Omitted): Omitted from the evaluation, creating an uncontrolled confound. Figure 4 classifies each dimension of for the nine studies; these states reflect our coding of what each paper controls, not quantity the papers report directly. Reporting requirements. For each comparison, researchers should report (i) the verification state of each dimension in R, (ii) the single-agent baselines strategy for matching compute (for example self-consistency with the same number of samples), (iii) the number of evaluation items, and (iv) binary outcomes for each item or paired statistics so that paired variance can be computed. Section 6 turns these into reviewer checklist. 11 Figure 4: Resource Accounting Matrix Across Primary Literature. Classification of experimental controls across all nine studies along the six dimensions of R: Strictly Controlled (identical budget enforced); Approximately Matched (bounded thresholds or iteration limits); Unmatched (audited but diverging); and Unreported (omitted).

sections.title: 6.1 What the evidence supports
sections.content: The evidence supports an empirical conclusion conditional on baseline strength. Against single greedy pass (Category A), multi-agent systems show an unweighted contrast mean of 0.032 across 358 contrasts (0.37 of contrasts ahead) and 0.010 weighted equally by study. Omitting Zhang et al., who supply 180 of these configurations, yields 0.005 contrast-weighted (0.48 ahead) and +0.003 weighted equally by study. Against sampled baselines (Category B; 360 contrasts), multiagent systems trail on average (0.051 contrast mean, 0.24 ahead; 0.038 without Zhang et al.). When thinking tokens or iterations are controlled (Category C; 114 contrasts), the average is 0.012 (0.024 study mean), and with matched thinking tokens single agents match or beat debate from 500 tokens upward. Across combined baselines matched on sample count or budget (474 contrasts across eight studies), the contrast mean is 0.042 (0.195 on log odds in REML). In 8 of 9 studies with equal compute or sampled baselines, the study mean is nonpositive. The sole positive exception among extracted studies is Wunderlich et al. [12], where debate (+0.013) and mixture-ofagents (+0.027) lead self-consistency at comparable compute read off Pareto fronts (not an exact budget match) on MMLU-Pro with Llama-3.1-70B (+0.020 mean; the mixture-of-agents proposers are copies of one model). In the cost audit, the mean multi-agent difference is 0.041 against self-consistency row with five samples and 0.007 against greedy chain-of-thought (Section 5).

sections.title: 6.2 Practitioner decision rules
sections.content: Rule 1: Exhaust single-agent search before introducing multi-agent topologies. Before engineering multi-agent communication pipelines, allocate equivalent inference compute to singleagent test-time scaling [68]. In deduction matched on thinking tokens, single agents match or outperform debate from 500 tokens upward; and under matching on agent count, majority voting without communication exceeds decentralized debate with two rounds (0.747 vs. 0.715) and, on average, the nine debate configurations of the same study. cost audit finds mean difference of 0.041 against row for self-consistency with five samples and 0.007 against greedy chain-ofthought (Section 5). In addition, borrowing the noise placebo control of Bertalaniˇc and Fortuna [17], injecting unrelated rationales under equal token volume allows researchers to separate semantic peer communication from raw prompt expansion. Rule 2: Deploy multiple agents based on task structure, not accuracy targets. Teams of agents are justifiable under specific structural constraints: input contexts exceeding context windows of single model, independent parallel tools, or sandboxed execution states. Kim et al. [10] report that multi-agent systems achieve gains on decomposable financial tasks but incur penalties on sequential software planning. MAS-Orchestra aligns with this pattern on ordered deduction tasks [34]. Under partial observability, communication topology affects token efficiency, reinforcing the need to audit communication overhead within [35]. Rule 3: Enforce external verification against ground truth. Agreement among model instances does not guarantee correctness, as language models struggle to verify their own outputs without external feedback [48]. Without compiler checks, unit tests, or database queries, multiagent debate risks propagating initial errors. On the SMFR benchmark with GPT-5, automated conversational graphs score between 20.2% and 63.0%, whereas tooling built by humans reaches 22 Figure 10: Four candidate mechanisms that can reduce multi-agent accuracy under equal compute. (1) Scaffold and echoed history reduce the budget left for reasoning (heuristic model of Section 3; not fitted to data). (2) Without external verification, errors can propagate across rounds. (3) Sequential rounds add latency, which none of the nine studies controls (Figure 4). (4) Greedy baselines credit coordination for gains that repeated sampling also provides. These mechanisms are hypotheses motivated by the evidence; this paper does not test them individually. 96.51%; the single-agent rows of the same table are 48.5% (CoT) and 57.0% (CoT-SC). Figure 10 diagrams these candidate failure modes, and Figure 11 maps the deployment flowchart.

sections.title: 6.3 The PACE Reviewer Checklist
sections.content: We propose reviewer checklist with six items for conference review guidelines: The PACE Reviewer Checklist for Multi-Agent LLM Submissions. 1. Resource vector with six dimensions: Does the submission report the verification status of all six resource dimensions: thinking tokens (Rreason), total tokens (Rtoken), dollar cost (Rcost), execution latency (Rlat), sample count (Rsample), and tool scaffolding (Rsys)? 2. Baselines with Equal Compute: When comparing against single agent, is the baseline allocated equal compute through self-consistency (CoT-SC), best-of-N , or extended reasoning tokens, rather than single greedy call? 3. Scaffold Accounting: Are system prompts, role headers, echoed message histories, and routing calls deducted from the multi-agent systems effective reasoning budget? 4. Following the Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE) protocol, we report the resource vector with six dimensions for every system. We compare our multi-agent system with both baseline with single pass (Category A, Greedy Single-Pass) and sample-matched or thinking-budget-matched single-agent baseline (Category B, Sampled Baseline, for example k-sample CoT-SC with equal to our number of agents), so that the coordination effect is separated from the effect of extra samples and test-time compute. sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Across 9 studies comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations, multi-agent systems show no consistent advantage once single-agent baselines receive repeated samples or matched compute budgets. Against baselines matched on sample count or budget the mean difference is 0.042 (REML ˆβ = 0.195, CR2 95% CI [0.320, 0.070]), and the multi-agent systems accuracy equals or falls below its baselines in 74% of the 474 contrasts  (Table 2)  . The one positive exception among extracted studies is Wunderlich et al. [12], at comparable compute read off Pareto fronts, not an exact budget match. The sampling gap is below zero in all 5 studies that report both baselines (Section 5.3). Architectural coordination cannot be demonstrated without holding test-time compute constant. Practitioners should allocate single agents equal inference budgets before deploying multi-agent pipelines, and reserve multi-agent topologies for tasks in which communication can add something. With shared evidence it adds no information (Proposition 3.1); it can help when the evidence is split across agents, when an external verifier filters changes, or when different models make different errors (Section 3.4).

sections.title: Open Science and Audit Trail
sections.content: Audit trail and data extraction. All 516 unique multi-agent configurations (across 531 raw extracted table rows) of the nine studies were extracted from primary source tables and verified through programmatic PDF concordance checks across the corpus (confirming all 336 cells in Tran and Kiela and page-level values across the remaining studies), alongside stratified 40-contrast audit (40 of 531 raw table rows, 7.5%, covering four to five contrasts per study across all nine studies in evidence/spot check ledger.md) inspected against the rendered primary tables with zero numerical discrepancies. Kim et al. values were additionally compared against the source-data file of the published version (see below). Item counts for the four added studies come from each papers text, with the basis recorded per row (stated, dataset size stated, derived, or estimated). Analysis protocol. The synthesis was not preregistered, and the analysis choices below were made while analyzing the extracted data, not fixed in advance. They are documented here for transparency: (i) the evidence base consists of nine studies (516 unique multi-agent configurations from 531 raw table rows), with five initial studies chosen to span different compute dimensions and four added studies selected from seven candidates screened against written criteria; (ii) descriptive summaries and sensitivity analyses are prioritized over inferential pooling because cluster-robust degrees of freedom are limited and matching condition is confounded with study; (iii) questions regarding capability thresholds are examined in light of task structure and baseline levels; (iv) studies are characterized along the resource vector R. Reference verification. The bibliography was audited against Crossref, OpenAlex, and arXiv records. The audit corrected author lists, titles, venues, and publication years, including for Kim et al., whose work appeared in Nature Machine Intelligence in 2026. Our extracted values for Kim et al.  (Table 16)  come from the arXiv preprint (v3). Comparing resolution rates with the source-data file of the published version shows 80 of 90 values agree; the other 10 values, for gemini-3-flash, are absent from that file and appear in Table S11 of the published supplement, matched by value but not by table position. Data and code availability. The analysis protocol, reproduction code, extraction tables (including contrasts_anchor5_core.csv and contrasts_dual_baseline.csv), the stratified audit ledger, the PACE Reviewer Checklist, and the evaluation utilities are publicly available at https://github.com/mahmoudsajjadi/pace and archived on Zenodo with an immutable DOI upon publication. sections.title: E Supplementary Sensitivity and Threshold Analyses
sections.content: The figures in the main text (Figures 1 to 11) present the baseline ladder, accounting decomposition, the theory phase diagram, resource matrix, evidence flow, empirical study ladder, SMFR frontier, the Category B/C REML estimates, scaling curves, failure taxonomy, and practitioner decision flow. This appendix reports supplementary sensitivity tables on all five Tran and Kiela arms and capability threshold diagnostics. E.1 Tran and Kiela: all five multi-agent arms The main analysis uses the Debate and Sequential arms of Tran and Kiela. Table 11 adds the subtask-parallel, parallel-roles, and ensemble arms against the same single-agent baseline at equal budgets of thinking tokens. Pooling all five arms gives mean difference of 0.017 over 240 contrasts, so arm selection does not change the conclusion. E.2 Threshold analysis: what was claimed Evaluating 260 configurations across six benchmarks published in Nature Machine Intelligence, Kim et al. [10] report capability saturation: on tasks where single-agent accuracy already exceeds approximately 45%, adding communicating agents yields negative returns across all four studied multi-agent topologies (Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid, Independent). They also report that coordination efficacy depends on task structure, ranging from gains on decomposable financial reasoning to losses on sequential software planning. The 45% figure represents ceiling on gains (agents help less, or degrade performance, once the baseline model is competent), rather than floor below which coordination fails. E.3 Why threshold claim is hard to establish Three methodological caveats apply to any hypothesis of capability threshold. First, accuracy is bounded in [0, 1], so absolute gains compress near the ceiling; apparent nonlinear breaks in raw accuracy differences can arise from measurement scale alone [33]. Testing requires metrics invariant to scale such as the log odds ratio. Second, baseline accuracy is confounded with task domain and model family: across existing studies, contrasts with high or low baseline accuracy originate from distinct benchmarks. Third, establishing that coordination fails at high capability requires compute matching; otherwise, gains at low baseline accuracy may reflect additional inference compute rather than communicative architecture. 41 Table 12: Mean accuracy difference (MAS SAS) for multi-agent contrasts with baseline accuracy below versus at or above 0.45, by study (m = 235 configurations excluding majority-voting baseline rows in Choi et al. and Wunderlich et al. The empirical pattern in Table 12 indicates that any capability threshold depends on domain and resource condition: In the study matched on thinking tokens (Tran and Kiela) and the cost audit (Jwalapuram et al.), accuracy differences stay near zero or negative on both sides of 0.45 (0.004 vs. 0.014 in Tran; 0.003 vs. 0.011 in Jwalapuram). These studies show no structural break dependent on baseline accuracy. In Kim et al.s tabulated contrasts (SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench), the pattern matches their reported ceiling: gains below 0.45 (+0.056) and losses above it (0.139). However, this table rests on = 20 instances per cell across nine model configurations, offering qualitative alignment rather than high statistical power. In Choi et al.s decentralized debate configurations (m = 14, excluding majority-voting rows treated as sampled baseline), differences remain positive against greedy decoding on both sides of 0.45 (+0.112 across two cells below 0.45, +0.034 across twelve cells at or above 0.45), reflecting unconstrained ensembling over five draws relative to single greedy pass. Pooling all four studies (m = 235) gives slope difference of +0.03 (HC3 standard error 0.17) between segments above and below the knot, showing no evidence of break. Kim et al. evaluate sequential tool-using tasks (code editing and terminal interaction) matched on iterations, attributing the ceiling to coordination overhead and error propagation when single agents are already capable. In contrast, Tran and Kiela evaluate multihop question answering matched on thinking tokens; there, single-agent reasoning matches or outperforms debate across nonvacuous budgets ( 500 tokens) regardless of baseline accuracy. Scaling across budgets in Tran and Kiela. At 100 thinking tokens, multi-agent debate holds an unweighted advantage ( = +0.077). However, the source authors document that 100 thinking tokens yield truncated reasoning outputs for both single-agent and multi-agent systems. At 500 tokens, the difference shifts to 0.012; from 1,000 to 10,000 tokens, single agents lead (0.023 to 0.035). Disaggregated scaling curves (Figure 9) show this pattern across both FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop deduction. E.6 Summary of the Threshold Evidence Three conclusions follow: (i) extracted data do not support universal capability threshold when reasoning tokens are matched; (ii) saturation in Kim et al. depends on task structure (present in sequential tool execution, absent in multihop deduction); and (iii) testing general scaling threshold requires scale-invariant metrics such as log odds ratios, resource accounting across R, and large item counts across continuous baseline accuracy variation.
